newsitem.title: UK: Unions urge BA strike talks, end fear tactics.
newsitem.headline: Unions urge BA strike talks, end fear tactics.

text.p: The Trades Union Congress (TUC), the main umbrella body for British unions, said on Thursday it was taking the 'very exceptional step' of calling on British Airways non-executive directors to resolve a dispute over pay between BA and cabin crew.

TUC general secretary John Monks, a moderate unionist, also expressed concern about the "unacceptable way" British Airways had handled the dispute" which, he said, was more about pursuing a 'union-busting' agenda than about an airline becoming more competitive.

His comments came at the end of the second day of strikes which have grounded hundreds of flights and stranded thousands of passengers. The spat -- over a new pay deal and a plan to save 42 million pounds -- enters its final day on Friday with no agreement in sight.

In a letter to nine board members and to chief executive Bob Ayling, Monks wrote: "BA staff, often anonymously for fear of retribution, have testified...in recent days about the fear they have been caused by the company's sustained and systematic campaign of personal harassment and intimidation."
BA's Ayling said in a statement he strongly rejected the TUC charge that BA had tried to intimidate its staff.
"My managers have rightly pointed out to our employees the consequences of taking strike action," he said.

BA management has warned that employees face loss of travel perks and opportunities of promotion if they went on strike. It has also threatened to sack or even sue individual strikers -- tactics which the unions have termed "intimidatory" and "macho".

Monks told the non-executives he hoped they would use their influence to allow a proper process of negotiation to take place to achieve the savings target set by the airline of 42 million pounds, "rather than piling threat upon threat to an already depressed and demoralised group of workers..."

He said the financial damage inflicted by the strike was considerable as well as the risk it posed to the company's standing with customers and staff morale. BA was imposing new terms and conditions on its workers rather than seeking agreement, he added.
Ayling however said its cost-savings programme had been fully discussed with all the members of the BA board and they supported it.

"The Board is in particular aware of the negotiations which took place over several months with the cabin crew unions and that BASSA (the British Airways Stewards and Stewardesses Association) rejected the need for 42 million pounds of savings by pay restructuring and walked out of the talks," Ayling said.
